item.title: Serving GLM-5.3 NVFP4 Across Two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM
item.description:
Serving GLM-5.3 NVFP4 Across Two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM

A tutorial demonstrates how to locally serve the NVIDIA GLM-5.3 NVFP4 model across two NVIDIA DGX Stations using vLLM and tensor parallelism. The setup connects both Stations over ConnectX-8 RDMA to serve requests through a single OpenAI-compatible API endpoint.

🔍 Overview

  • Model Scale: NVIDIA GLM-5.3 NVFP4 is a quantized version of Z.ai’s mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, containing 753 billion parameters with 40 billion parameters activated per token.
  • Memory Challenge: The model checkpoint requires approximately 464 GB of storage, exceeding the 252 GB of HBM3e memory available on a single GB300 GPU.
  • GPU-Only Execution: Sparse activation reduces token computation, but all weights must remain accessible because tokens route to different experts. Using two DGX Stations keeps all model weights in GPU memory with CPU weight offloading disabled.

🧩 How It Works

  • Tensor Parallelism (TP=2): Splits the model’s weights and computation evenly across the two GB300 GPUs.
  • Node Roles: Station A (rank 0) hosts the OpenAI-compatible API server. Station B (rank 1) acts strictly as a worker node without an API server.
  • Request Execution: Both Stations compute every incoming request simultaneously. Station A returns the final answer through the API endpoint.
  • Interconnect Validation: The Stations communicate via ConnectX-8 RDMA over two direct rails (cx8r0 and cx8r1). Pre-deployment checks confirm device mapping (such as mlx5_1) and IPv4 addressing to prevent NCCL timeouts.

⚙️ Key System Requirements

Component / Requirement Description
Hardware Two GB300 DGX Stations running Linux, validated via the Connect Two DGX Stations playbook and GPU-memory RDMA test
Storage At least 464 GB of free disk space per Station for the model checkpoint, container image, and temporary files
Container Image vllm/vllm-openai:v0.30.0-aarch64@sha256:4864d46625cbc3307623e29ac742030655e27249feba7b97ec925ce4cc4dfb56
Model Source Repository nvidia/GLM-5.3-NVFP4 (revision e3b8f9f2fad29727dfa95e766c5cac18ea1414bf) stored at $HOME/models/GLM-5.3-NVFP4
User Access SSH and sudo access on both Stations using the same Linux username; docker group membership
License & Datasets Acceptance of NVIDIA Open Model Agreement, original GLM-5.3 license, SPEED-Bench (under NVIDIA Evaluation Dataset License Agreement), and access to Hugging Face gated dataset cais/hle

#vLLM #NVIDIA #DGXStation #TensorParallelism #MixtureOfExperts #LLMInference

Source: When One GPU Isn’t Enough: Serving GLM-5.3 Across Two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: ADIndex Accelerates Token-Level Sparse Attention Indexing in Long-Context LLM Inference
item.description:
ADIndex Accelerates Token-Level Sparse Attention Indexing in Long-Context LLM Inference

ADIndex has been introduced as an adaptive and distillation-driven indexing method designed to resolve latency bottlenecks in token-level sparse attention architectures such as DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA). While DSA lowers computational costs via token-level selection, its indexer scores the entire causal prefix for each query, making indexing a primary source of latency in long-context inference.

🔍 Overview

DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) reduces the computational cost of attention by selecting tokens. However, its indexer evaluates the full causal prefix for every query, causing indexing to dominate latency during long-context workloads. At long context lengths, the indexer alone can account for more than 50% of total prefill GPU time. ADIndex addresses this computational bottleneck to make sparse attention indexing more efficient.

🧩 How it works

ADIndex incorporates three main components to optimize token-level sparse attention indexing:

  • Layer-wise calibration strategy: Adaptively accommodates cross-query retrieval overlap, motivated by observations of pronounced inter-layer heterogeneity.
  • Group-level distillation scheme: Leverages inter-layer heterogeneity to efficiently train adaptive layer-wise group indexers that capture salient retrieval signals from individual queries.
  • Low-latency inference strategy: Reduces repeated full-prefix scans by sharing token banks within query groups while retaining query-specific refinement.

⚙️ Key details

Experiments evaluating ADIndex on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1 show significant efficiency improvements over standard DSA while preserving accuracy:

  • Task performance: Maintains near-lossless performance on LongBench, LongBench v2, and RULER benchmarks.
  • Prefill kernel speedup: Achieves up to a 6.22x speedup at a context length of 256K across layer-wise reuse configurations.
  • Decoding kernel speedup: Delivers up to a 3.40x speedup at a context length of 256K across layer-wise reuse configurations.
  • End-to-end serving speedup: Reaches a 1.54x speedup at a context length of 128K.

#ADIndex #DeepSeek #SparseAttention #LLMInference #ModelOptimization

Source: ADIndex: Layer-Adaptive Sparse Attention Indexing via Group-Level Distillation Source: TimeOmni-o1: Bidirectionally Coupling Time Series Foundation Models and LLMs for Multimodal Reasoning and Forecasting Source: One Byte, One Token: Byteifying a 27B Hybrid-Attention LLM with Self-Generated Data

item.title: Fused MoE Kernel Optimizes Decode Performance on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs
item.description:
Fused MoE Kernel Optimizes Decode Performance on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs

Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE) models boost LLM capacity while keeping per‑token compute low, but the decode phase suffers from high latency because the underlying GPU kernels are inefficient.

🔍 Overview

  • MoE is a sparsely‑activated architecture that scales large language model capacity while keeping per‑token compute low.
  • MoE operations make up a large share of total compute time, so inefficiencies directly raise request latency and cost.
  • Optimizing MoE operations through kernel engineering offers the largest opportunity for performance gains.

🧩 How MoE and Fused Kernels Work

  • Fused MoE merges token routing, data shuffling, and specialized network calculations into a single batched GPU operation, replacing separate sequential loop operations.
  • This fusion provides latency advantages but adds complexity to kernel implementation and debugging.

⚙️ Hopper WGMMA Constraints

  • NVIDIA Hopper uses the Warp Group Matrix Multiply‑Accumulate (WGMMA) instruction, executed across a cooperative warp‑group of 128 threads.
  • In the wgmma.mma_async definition, the hardware fixes the matrix row dimension M to 64, defining the thread‑mapping topology.
  • Operand A must occupy this fixed M = 64 dimension (using registers or shared memory); Operand B occupies the variable N dimension via a shared‑memory descriptor.
  • The operand slots are structurally non‑interchangeable, and peak tile utilization requires M ≥ 64.
  • The hardware enforces a minimum layout shape for the leading dimension of the first operand, locking the block height to exactly 64 rows.

Table: Operand Mapping on Hopper WGMMA

Operand Fixed/Variable Dimension Mapping Requirement
A Fixed M = 64 rows Must fill a 64‑row layout bucket
B Variable N dimension Can be large (e.g., 8192)

📈 Decoding Bottleneck and the Flip Technique

  • Decode processes a single token per user sequence, yielding a thin batch dimension M (often M < 64, sometimes M = 1).
  • Matrix A becomes a thin vector (e.g., 1 × 4096), while matrix B (expert weights) remains a large dense block (e.g., 4096 × 8192).
  • Because M is tiny, A cannot fill the hardware’s 64‑row layout, leaving many Tensor Core lanes idle and causing poor utilization.
  • MoE layers fracture the workload across many experts, making them especially sensitive to these constraints.
  • For a topk=8 routine, the effective N dimension inside the fused kernel expands to tens or hundreds of thousands of parameters.
  • Flipping the multiplication (transposing the matrices before PTX assembly) moves the large expert dimension N = 8192 into the first operand position, satisfying the mandatory 64‑row requirement and unlocking hardware prefetching.
  • This re‑alignment matches the exact topography of Hopper silicon, allowing the expansive N dimension to flood the required rows and dramatically improve hardware utilization.

💡 Why It Matters

  • By addressing the structural asymmetry of Hopper’s WGMMA instruction, the fused MoE kernel reduces decode latency.
  • Better utilization of Tensor Core capacity lowers the compute cost of serving MoE‑based LLMs.
  • The technique enables MoE models to retain their capacity‑scaling benefits without incurring prohibitive inference overhead.

#MixtureOfExperts #HopperGPU #KernelOptimization #LLMInference

Source: Mixture-of-Experts kernel engineering on Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services

item.title: KVFetch adds temporal recall channel to improve KV‑cache compression
item.description:
KVFetch adds temporal recall channel to improve KV‑cache compression

KVFetch: Temporal Prefetching for the Missing Half of KV Cache Compression was submitted on 23 Sep 2026. It introduces a new mechanism to address a key limitation of current KV‑cache compressors used during long‑context LLM inference.

🔍 Overview

  • As context windows grow to tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens, KV‑cache compression becomes essential for efficient inference.
  • Existing compressors belong to three families: score‑based eviction, summary compensation, and offload‑and‑recall.
  • All three decide what to keep or recall solely by content relevance to the current query.

⚙️ Problem with existing KV‑cache compressors

  • A cache supports two access modes: associative lookup by content and sequential traversal by position.
  • Current compressors implement only the associative (content‑based) mode.
  • This omission matters for tasks such as retrieval‑augmented generation, code completion, and structured‑data extraction, which need verbatim reproduction of identifiers, field values, or code tokens.
  • Under compression, content‑based eviction keeps the head of a sequence but discards its continuation, causing “sequential forgetting” – a failure that persists despite better scoring, larger budgets, summary compensation, or dynamic re‑scoring.
  • Sequential forgetting is identified as the dominant source of remaining quality loss under compression.

🛠️ KVFetch design

  • KVFetch is a training‑free, drop‑in framework that adds a temporal recall channel to any score‑based compressor.
  • It demotes evicted candidates to a quantized cold tier.
  • It detects active copying through a monotone read pointer.
  • It prefetches positional successors into fixed‑size hot‑tier slots without increasing attention cost.

📊 Results

  • Evaluation on RULER‑16K under an iso‑budget control shows:
    • Verbatim copying recovery improves from 0.8 % to 78.4 %.
    • The 13‑task average score rises by +8.4 points, with gains concentrated on tasks requiring sequential access.
  • On LongBench, where no task requires sequential access, the temporal channel stays dormant and imposes no cost.

🚀 Availability

  • KVFetch is presented as a drop‑in framework, implying it can be incorporated into existing score‑based compressors without additional training.
  • The work is hosted on arXiv Labs, a platform that encourages community collaboration and upholds values of openness, community, excellence, and user data privacy.

The story is based on the arXiv preprint titled “KVFetch: Temporal Prefetching for the Missing Half of KV Cache Compression.”

#KVCache #LLMInference #Compression

Source: KVFetch: Temporal Prefetching for the Missing Half of KV Cache Compression Source: Task-Oriented Key-Layer KV Communication for Efficient Latent Multi-Agent Collaboration Source: Algorithmic Scratchpads and Curriculum Staging for Arithmetic Reasoning in Tiny Transformers Source: SPIN: Shadow Predictive Indexer for Sparse Attention Source: A Self-Pruning Transformer: Extreme KV-Cache Compression with Universal Attention Source: LRCC: Generalizing Low-Rank Compression with Conditional Computation Source: OnlineQAT: On-Policy Distillation for Ultra-Low-Bit Large Language Models

item.title: NVIDIA Blackwell Confidential Computing retains up to 98% LLM inference throughput
item.description:
NVIDIA Blackwell Confidential Computing retains up to 98% LLM inference throughput

NVIDIA demonstrated that running a 32K‑input/1K‑output LLM inference workload inside confidential virtual machines (CVMs) on a Blackwell‑based DGX B200 system keeps almost all of the baseline performance.

🔍 Overview

NVIDIA Confidential Computing (CC) provides memory‑encrypted CVMs, confidential GPUs, and encrypted NVLink, enabling LLM inference to run securely while preserving throughput.

🧩 How it works

  • Secure data path – The Blackwell CC architecture enforces hardware‑based protection for data and workloads in use.
  • Host‑to‑device transfer – In the B200 CC, transfers go through a software‑encrypted bounce buffer because the GPU cannot directly access protected CVM memory.
  • TensorRT LLM adaptations
    • Uses CC‑aware memory selection, opting for pageable memory on protected paths instead of always using pinned memory.
    • Moves repeated‑token and sampling‑data readback to an asynchronous worker, so protected copies do not block the main scheduler during decode.
    • Measures tactics with the GPU %globaltimer inside CC while keeping CUDA events outside CC.
  • NVLink limitation – NVLS (NVLink SHARP) multicast is not available in B200 CC configurations.

⚙️ Key details

  • Model: nvidia/DeepSeek-R1-0528-NVFP4
  • Inference framework: TensorRT LLM (Docker container) with PyTorch backend
  • Sequence lengths: 32K input, 1K output
  • Parallelism: TP=8, EP=1, PP=1; KV cache in FP8
  • Concurrency tested: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 requests
  • Hardware: 1 NVIDIA DGX B200 system (8 NVIDIA B200 GPUs), GPU power limit 1,000 W
  • Platform: Intel TDX
  • Host OS / kernel: Ubuntu 25.10 / 6.17.0-20-generic
  • Guest OS / kernel: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS / 6.8.0-124-generic, 256 vCPUs, 2 NUMA nodes
  • Driver / software stack: NVIDIA driver 595.71.05, VBIOS FW 1.4.x, CUDA 13.2, TensorRT LLM 1.3.0rc22, NCCL v2.30, OpenSSL 3.6.0, Docker + NVIDIA Container Toolkit

📈 Performance results

  • Across concurrency levels 1–16, CC retained 96.1 %–98.2 % of the output‑token throughput compared with a non‑confidential baseline.
  • Mean TPOT (time‑per‑output‑token) stayed within 1.2 %–4.3 % of the baseline.
  • These results show that the security overhead of CC is limited to a few percent while providing full data protection.

💡 Why it matters

The Blackwell confidential computing architecture creates a hardware‑enforced security path that protects data in use without sacrificing most of the inference performance required for large‑scale LLM deployments.

#NVIDIA #ConfidentialComputing #LLMInference

Source: Enabling Private High-Performance Production AI Inference with NVIDIA Confidential Computing | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Amazon SageMaker AI Introduces Concurrency Sweeps for Generative AI Endpoints
item.description:
Amazon SageMaker AI Introduces Concurrency Sweeps for Generative AI Endpoints

Amazon SageMaker AI has updated its Inference Recommendations to include concurrency sweeps, a systematic benchmarking approach used to right-size generative AI endpoints by optimizing price-performance while maintaining acceptable latency.

🔍 Overview

A concurrency sweep sends controlled, increasing levels of simultaneous requests to a SageMaker AI endpoint to analyze performance. This feature is built into Amazon SageMaker AI Inference Recommendations, eliminating the need to build or maintain custom load-testing infrastructure.

🧩 How it works

The concurrency sweep measures two primary metrics at each level of traffic:

  • Throughput: The number of tokens per second produced by the endpoint.
  • Latency: The time taken for each request.

The workflow consists of four steps:

  1. Deploy the model to a SageMaker AI endpoint using the native vLLM container.
  2. Configure the workload profile (input and output token counts, streaming mode).
  3. Run the concurrency sweep using the CreateAIBenchmarkJob API.
  4. Analyze the results to identify optimal concurrency and right-size the fleet.

⚙️ Key details

In a deployment scenario using the NVIDIA Nemotron-3 Nano 30B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model on an ml.g7e.2xlarge instance (backed by an NVIDIA Blackwell GPU), the following configurations are applied:

Configuration Detail
Container vLLM Deep Learning Container for SageMaker AI
SM_VLLM_ENFORCE_EAGER Required for Nemotron-3 Nano’s Mamba-Transformer hybrid architecture
GPU Memory Utilization Set to 0.85 to provide headroom for KV cache growth
Prefix Caching Enabled to reuse cached key-value pairs for repeated system prompts

Workload profiles are defined using CreateAIWorkloadConfig with the following parameters:

Parameter Value Description
prompt_input_tokens_mean 1,024 Average input prompt length
output_tokens_mean 256 Average generated response length

Streaming is enabled to capture time to first token (TTFT) metrics for interactive user experiences. The benchmark engine (AIPerf) runs each concurrency level sequentially within a single job, sending the total number of requests defined under request_count at each level.

#AmazonSageMaker #vLLM #GenerativeAI #LLMInference #NVIDIA

Source: Right-size generative AI endpoints with concurrency sweeps on Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Optimizing Speculative Decoding Draft Length for LLM Inference
item.description:
Optimizing Speculative Decoding Draft Length for LLM Inference

Speculative decoding is a technique for accelerating the autoregressive decoding phase of LLM inference by predicting multiple tokens per iteration. New guidelines detail how to optimize draft length based on workload characteristics and hardware constraints, particularly for mixture-of-experts models and attention-heavy workloads.

🔍 Overview

Speculative decoding works by using a small draft model to predict several likely next tokens, which are then verified in parallel with a single pass through the larger target model. This approach reduces the total number of decoding iterations while increasing the arithmetic intensity of the target model, without requiring higher concurrency.

The target model accepts the proposed tokens in sequence until it encounters the first mismatch. The next prediction cycle then resumes from that position. Because only tokens accepted by the target model are retained, speculative decoding produces the same output sequence as standard decoding, unless the acceptance criteria are deliberately relaxed.

🧩 Key Metrics

  • Draft length (\(D\)): The number of proposed tokens per target iteration
  • Acceptance length (\(AL\)): The number of tokens produced (accepted) per target iteration
  • \(AL\) ranges from \(1\) to \((1 + D)\) because the target can always produce one new ground-truth token in addition to the accepted draft tokens

⚙️ Compute and Memory Dynamics

During verification, compute scales with \((1 + D)\), but memory access remains unchanged. The goal is to increase \(D\) until \(T_{\mathrm{verif}}\) remains constant, typically up to the point where verification transitions from memory bound to compute bound.

With speculation, the GEMM-\(M\) for each target linear layer GEMM grows from \(M\) to \(M \times (1 + D)\), where \(M\) is the GEMM-\(M\) with no speculation.

Draft length Batch size reduction for compute-bound
\(D=7\) One-eighth of batch size needed vs. \(D=0\)

As mixture-of-experts (MoE) models become sparser and long-context workloads increase KV capacity pressure, the effective concurrency per expert decreases, making larger draft lengths attractive across the Pareto frontier.

📐 Three Guidelines for Draft Length Selection

Guideline 1: Increase speculative decoding draft length to push GEMMs into the compute-bound region without increasing KV cache capacity pressure.

Guideline 2: When attention dominates decode time, choose \(D = \frac{128}{G} – 1\).

For reasoning and agentic workloads, attention tends to dominate the execution time in the throughput-oriented region. On current GPU devices, attention kernels achieve good hardware utilization at GEMM-\(M=128\). The \(G = 32\) variant reaches throughput saturation at a lower value of \(D\). Beyond the throughput saturation point, attention is no longer DRAM bandwidth bound, and its runtime scales with \(D\).

Guideline 3: If you choose \(D > \frac{128}{G} – 1\), prefer values where \(G \times (1 + D)\) is a multiple of 128 to avoid tile underutilization.

Attention runtime also depends on tile size. Runtime increases in steps as \(G \times (1 + D)\) crosses a multiple of 128, the software tile size for the benchmarked attention kernel. If \(G \times (1 + D)\) falls between two tile boundaries, the last tile is only partially utilized but still costs about as much as a full tile.

📊 Performance Characteristics

  • With \(D=7\), one-eighth of the batch size is needed to become compute bound compared to \(D=0\)
  • Normalized attention throughput varies with \(D\) for different \(G\) values across 32K and 128K KV sequence lengths
  • Attention kernel tile size is 128

#speculativedecoding #LLMinference #mixtureofexperts #GPUoptimization #attentionmechanism #GEMMoptimization

Source: Co-Designing AI Models Using Speculative Decoding for Faster LLM Inference | NVIDIA Technical Blog
